steps.body: The angles you'll meet constantly are clean fractions of the anchor: **30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2**. The pattern: the denominator tells how many copies fit in 180°. Six 30s, four 45s, three 60s, two 90s — the smaller the angle, the BIGGER the denominator.

widget.prompt: Match each degree measure to its radian form.

pairErrors.feedback: π/4 is 45° — four of those fill 180. Thirty degrees needs SIX copies: π/6.
2π/3 is 120° — two 60° steps. Ninety degrees is half the anchor: π/2.

widget.missFeedback: Read each denominator as “how many fit in 180°.”
widget.successFeedback: The four workhorse angles, both languages — these unlock the whole unit circle.

explanationVariants: 135° is three 45° steps, and each step is π/4: so 135° = 3π/4, n = 3.

commonErrors.feedback: n = 4 gives 4π/4 = π = 180° — a step too far. 135° is three 45s: n = 3.
n = 6 gives 6π/4 = 270° — way past. Count 45° steps: 135/45 = 3.

steps.body: Reading π-fractions BACK is the same skill reversed: treat the denominator as a step size and count. π/6 steps are 30° each, so 5π/6 is five 30° steps: 150°. No formula grinding — just steps of a known size.

commonErrors.feedback: 30° is a single π/6 step — the 5 got dropped. Five steps of 30°: 150°.
210° is 7π/6 — one step overcounted. Five 30° steps stop at 150°.

explanationVariants: π/2 steps are quarter turns — three of them reach three-quarters of the circle.

commonErrors.feedback: 90° is one π/2 step — there are THREE: 270°.
540 is 3 × 180 — the /2 went missing. Each step is π/2 = 90°, so 3 × 90 = 270°.

steps.body: Angles don't stop at one lap. A negative angle turns CLOCKWISE, and an angle past 2π keeps spinning — a full turn plus a quarter turn lands exactly where the quarter turn does. The landing spot repeats every 2π; the total rotation is what the number records.

widget.prompt: A wheel turns one FULL turn plus a quarter turn. Total rotation in radians? (Round to hundredths.)

commonErrors.feedback: 6.28 is the full turn ALONE — the quarter turn (π/2 ≈ 1.57) still adds on: ≈ 7.85.
1.57 is only the quarter turn — the full 2π lap counts too: 2π + π/2 ≈ 7.85.

explanationVariants: −5π/6 is five 30° steps, run CLOCKWISE (the negative sign): −150°.
Same size steps as the positive 5π/6 (150°) — the sign only flips the direction, not the count.

widget.prompt: Same size steps as before, but this angle runs clockwise: −5π/6. What degree measure is that?

commonErrors.feedback: 150° drops the direction — the negative sign means clockwise, so the degree measure is negative too: −150°.
−30° is a single clockwise step — the 5 got dropped. Five clockwise steps of 30°: −150°.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 5 × 30° = 150°, and the negative sign flips the direction: −150°.

hints: Each π/6 step is still 30° in size — count five of them.
The MINUS sign is the only new thing: it means clockwise, from C3.

takeaways: 30-45-60-90 ↔ π/6, π/4, π/3, π/2 — denominators count copies in 180°.
Read nπ/d as n steps of size 180/d degrees.
Angles run negative (clockwise) and past 2π (extra laps).
steps.teaser: Next: the payoff formula radians were built for — arc length.

concept.body: One π-fraction, decoded. 60° fits into 180° exactly three times, so 60° = π/3 — the denominator IS the count of copies. Ask “how many of this angle fill 180?” and the radian form writes itself.

explanationVariants: Smaller angles need bigger denominators — 30° takes π/6.

commonErrors.feedback: π/6 is 30° — that denominator counts SIX copies in 180°. Sixty-degree copies number three: π/3.
The denominator counts copies in 180°, not the degree value itself: 180/60 = 3.
